# El verdadero premio de emprender — Santiago Magnín

**Internal note, not public copy.** No credit line: public text uses our own words and names.
**Link to original:** ⬜ add YouTube URL.
**Source used:** auto-generated transcript pasted by Bruno (2026-09-30). The transcript stops
mid-sentence and has numerical errors. Re-watch before quoting anything.

## What it teaches (paraphrased)

The question: *what's a reasonable reward for starting something and doing well, and what
reward can't be sustained even though many people get it in the short run?*

1. **Perseverance vs. obstinacy** is a thin line. His own curve: years of results under his
   employee opportunity cost, then a business model that clicked, then fast growth that
   decelerates. From inside year one, it looked identical to wasting time. Some people stay
   in years of "rowing in dulce de leche" on something that will never work. The honest
   answer is sometimes *"this doesn't work, stop."*
2. **Measure against opportunity cost.** He compounded the gap between what he earned and what
   a salaried job would have paid, to check whether the effort ever paid off.
3. **Compare against a safe baseline.** Safest: US Treasuries (considered risk-free
   *because they always pay*, not because their price never moves). Then diversified bonds, then
   50/50, then 100% stocks. Higher average return, deeper worst years.
4. **Averages lie about the path.** A 6% "long-run" bond portfolio still had consecutive
   losing years; 100% stocks can be down ~half intra-year. "Hay que tener mucha psiquis."
5. **If a diversified portfolio can fall ~50%, a single company (your own) can fall to zero.**
   Concentration is what makes entrepreneurship dangerous. (Transcript ends here.)

## What we adopted → where in the map

| Idea | Fit | Proposed landing spot |
|---|---|---|
| **Perseverance vs. obstinacy** | Persona + brand pillar; also a *habit* cairn | Ch. 1 (1.1.3 "Seguí registrando"): how to know the habit is working; Ch. 2 review |
| **Measure vs. a baseline** (opportunity cost) | Method for "am I doing OK?" | Ch. 4: compare your return with a simple baseline (inflación / UVA / MEP) |
| **Risk ladder** (safe → bonds → mixed → stocks) | Core of Ch. 4 teaching | Ch. 4.1 teaching concepts; a "¿cuánta caída aguantás?" cairn |
| **Averages hide bad years** | Anti-humo honesty | Ch. 4 copy rule: always show a bad-year example next to the average |
| **Concentration risk** | Risk principle | Ch. 5.0 portfolio (don't put everything in one thing, incl. your own business) |

## Argentine rework

- Replace "US Treasuries = risk-free" with the local analog carefully: there is **no risk-free
  peso asset**; the closest anchor is **dólar / UVA-linked / short-term instruments**, with
  explicit caveats. This needs care and verification before any claim.
- The "bad year" in Argentina isn't a 20% stock dip; it's a devaluation or inflation jump.
  Use *local* bad years as the stress example.

## What we do NOT copy

- His business figures (yearly % growth, subscriber counts).
- US bond/stock statistics as if they applied to Argentine savers.
- The "keep going" framing without the "or stop" half; the honest version is our edge against
  *humo*.
